To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the grain size of olivine in the mantle wedge increases from 10 μm at the slab surface to a few centimeter at the bottom of the wedge, with only a minor effect on the mantle flow.

grain-size-dependent rheology and grain-size evolution in the mantle wedge lead to a characteristic downdip grain-size distribution, which is consistent with the seismic structure of the mantle wedge at most subduction zones.

grain size increases from ∼10 to 100 microns in the most trenchward portion of the subduction zone to several centimeters in the mantle wedge and that the grain-size increase leads to a ∼5 order of magnitude increase in permeability in the subarc wedge, which is likely to promote the upward migration of aqueously derived fluids and melts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of grain-size-dependent rheology on subduction-zone mantle flow and fluid transport.
the effect of grain-size evolution on the rheology, flow, and fluid migration in the subducting mantle.
the grain-size distribution and its effect on the rheology and flow in the mantle wedge.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the grain size is not an important parameter to consider in the mantle flow and melt migration models of subduction zones. [2]

the mantle wedge is a highly heterogeneous system with respect to mineral grain-size distribution, and that the grain-size distribution has a significant impact on the mantle rheological and transport properties.
the mantle wedge is composed of a composite olivite rheology that incorporates both grain-size-dependent diffusion and grain-size-independent (i.e., dislocation) creep.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the characteristic grain size in the mantle wedge is controlled primarily by the thermal and tectonic setting of subduction zones and that it is relatively insensitive to the details of grain-size evolution.
grain size plays an indirect, rather than direct, role in controlling mantle flow in the subduction zone.

the grain-size distribution is controlled by the thermal field and mantle flow in the wedge, and the grain size in the subarc wedge is large enough to accommodate most of the deformation by dislocation creep.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mantle flow and fluid dynamics are strongly coupled in the mantle wedge. [2]

the grain-size distribution is a natural consequence of the thermal and dynamic conditions in the subduction zone, with little dependence on the details of the grain-size evolution model or the rheology.
the grain-size distribution predicted by the coupled flow and grain-size model is a robust result and can be used to constrain mantle processes at subduction zones.
